context: The caption says “binary search tree,” but the figure actually shows an ordinary binary tree. The left child of root 1 is 2, greater than the root, violating the search tree ordering that puts smaller values on the left and larger ones on the right. The inorder output here is therefore not in ascending order.
The tree has 7 nodes. Root 1 has left child 2 and right child 3. Node 2 has left child 4 and right child 5, and 3 has left child 6 and right child 7. Nodes 4, 5, 6, and 7 are leaves.
description: The dashed line around the tree traces depth-first recursive calls and returns, rather than parent-child edges. At each node, an orange dot on the left marks preorder (before left recursion), a blue dot below marks inorder (between left and right recursion), and a purple dot on the right marks postorder (after right recursion).

frames.explanation: All three traversals recurse into the left subtree first, then the right, and return immediately at a null node. They differ in when the current node is recorded. The table lists the recording point, visit order, and output for each traversal.
frames.title: Three depth-first traversals of a binary tree

summary: Preorder, inorder, and postorder follow the same depth-first recursive path. They differ in when they record the current node's value.

headers: When to record the current node
